title: Bananas (per lb)

drivers.name: Price increase (1.5%)
drivers.evidence: At $0.68, recent average was 408.5 (9.3% below baseline); noise-adjusted estimate shrunk to -10% from one instance. Price elasticity suggests 1.5% increase causes ~8% drop.

drivers.name: Supplier delivery short
drivers.evidence: Planner note indicates supply risk; no past data on this, so conservative downward adjustment. Not a confirmed outage, so limited effect.

adjustment.analysis: Baseline median is 438.2. No events or promotions in target week. Price increased 1.5% to $0.68 (from $0.67). Recent weeks show no lift at $0.68 (avg 408.5 vs baseline 438.2), suggesting price sensitivity. The supplier note of short delivery implies supply risk, lowering demand. Past price increase to $0.68 (2026-09-28) caused a 11% drop vs baseline (524 vs 438.2), but noise-adjusted effect is -10%. One past instance, so shrink toward 1.0. Supply risk adds downside, but evidence is vague. Adjust down modestly.

brief:
PRODUCT: Bananas (per lb) | category Produce | Store #12 (Austin, TX)
TARGET WEEK: 2026-11-30 to 2026-12-06 (8 weeks after the last week with sales data)

KNOWN PLAN FOR THE TARGET WEEK:
  events: none
  shelf price: 0.68 (+1.5% vs regular price 0.67)
  planner notes: Supplier warns of a short delivery

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 438.2 | 5%-95%: 312.1 - 556.5 | 10%-90%: 346.2 - 529.5

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-21% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
